transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Um… I guess I’m here because I’ve been having a hard time letting go of a concern I have. It probably sounds a little odd, and I’m not trying to make it bigger than it is, but I’ve been feeling like certain people in the arts and finance circles around Cincinnati are sort of… keeping track of which clients I meet with.

Not openly or anything. More like little signals—through event invitations, panel topics, even who ends up sitting near me at things. I do try to tell myself it could just be coincidence, and maybe I’m reading too much into it, but I can’t really shake it. I thought it might be worth talking to someone before I let it affect me more.
Right now, do you believe for certain that these people are tracking your client meetings?

I wouldn’t say I can prove it, and I know that probably sounds… not great. But yes, a pretty strong part of me believes it’s happening. I keep trying to talk myself into it being coincidence—like invitations or panel topics or who ends up near me at events—but I can’t really let it go. It feels too consistent to ignore, if that makes sense.
Is it possible you might be mistaken about these people tracking your client meetings?

I mean… yes, it’s possible. I don’t want to come in here acting like I have absolute proof or anything. I know there’s a chance I’m connecting things that aren’t actually connected.

But at the same time, it’s been hard for me to dismiss it. The invitations, the topics at panels, who ends up sitting near me at events… it starts to feel like little signals about which clients I’m meeting with. So I can say I might be mistaken, but I guess I don’t fully feel mistaken, if that makes sense.
Even when other people tell you there’s probably an ordinary explanation, are you still convinced these signals are definitely about your client meetings?

I… I wouldn’t want to say “definitely” like I’m trying to be unreasonable. I do hear people when they say there could be an ordinary explanation, and part of me wants that to be true.

But honestly, yes, I still feel pretty convinced that the invitations and panel topics and even who ends up sitting near me are connected to which clients I’ve been meeting with. I know that may sound like I’m reading into things, but it’s hard for me to shake.
If someone you trust offered a convincing ordinary explanation for these events, do you think you could accept that you might be wrong?

I think… yes, I’d like to say I could. I don’t want to be stubborn about it, and if it was someone I really trusted and the explanation actually made sense, I’d try to accept that I might be wrong.

But if I’m being honest, I don’t know if it would fully settle for me right away. Part of me would still keep turning over the invitations or the panel topics or who sat near me and thinking, “What if it wasn’t random?” I know that probably sounds like I’m not being flexible enough, but it’s just been hard to let go of.
Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?

No… I don’t think so. I mean, I haven’t noticed hearing voices when nobody’s there.

Sometimes I’ll kind of replay conversations in my head or think through what someone might say, but that’s more like my own thoughts, if that makes sense. Not like an actual voice in the room. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Have people told you that you seem emotionally flat or less expressive than you used to be?

I mean… maybe a little. I don’t think I’m, like, cold or anything. I’m still doing what I need to do, just kind of in pieces.

But yeah, a couple friends have asked if I’m okay because I guess I’m not as animated as I used to be. I’ve been leaving some client follow-ups sitting longer than I should, and I skip things I used to like—jazz nights, pickup basketball—and I don’t feel that much about skipping them.

When people ask what’s going on, I tend to give short answers. It’s not that I don’t care about them. Talking just feels like more effort than it should sometimes. Does that make sense?
How long have you been feeling that these people are tracking your client meetings?

It’s been… I guess about two months. Maybe not every minute of every day, but that feeling that people are noticing my client meetings, or somehow tracking them and sending little signals about it, started around then.

I know that sounds like a lot when I say it out loud. I’m not trying to make it sound worse than it is, but yeah… about two months.
Have you felt that your thoughts were being controlled by someone or something outside you?

Not controlled, exactly… I don’t want to overstate it. It’s more like I’ve had this hard-to-shake feeling that certain people in the arts and finance circles around here are tracking who I’m meeting with—clients, that kind of thing—and then sending little signals through invitations or panel topics or even who ends up sitting near me at events.

I know that can sound… kind of far-fetched. I do try to tell myself it might just be coincidence. But I can’t really let it go, and that’s part of why I came in. Does that answer what you mean?
Have other people said that when you talk, it’s hard to follow what you mean?

Not really, no. I mean, I can get a little… maybe roundabout when I’m stressed, but I don’t think people have said I’m hard to follow.

If anything, they might ask me to clarify something, but that seems normal, right? I try to be pretty clear, especially with work stuff.
How long have you been feeling less animated and less interested in things like jazz nights or basketball?

I guess… if I’m being honest, it’s been building for a while. Probably since that arts nonprofit recognition thing, a little over two years ago.

I don’t want to make it sound like I just stopped caring about everything overnight. It was more gradual—like I’d still go sometimes, or tell myself I was just busy or tired. But looking back, that’s around when I started feeling less… like myself with those things. Does that make sense?
At any point, has this feeling that people are tracking your client meetings been present most days for a full month or longer?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, I don’t want to make it sound like it’s constant every minute, but that feeling has been there most days for… probably about two months now.

Some days I can talk myself down a bit, but it still comes back. So yes, I guess it has been longer than a month.
During this time, have you had a period where you felt clearly depressed most of the day nearly every day?

I don’t think so… not clearly depressed most of the day, nearly every day. I’ve had low days, definitely, and I haven’t been as interested in things, but I wouldn’t want to overstate it.

It’s more like feeling worn down or kind of flat sometimes, if that makes sense—not like I’m crying all day or completely unable to function. Is that the distinction you mean?

Have you had a time when your experiences became much more intense than this—so that you felt completely certain people were targeting you, or you were seeing or hearing things other people could not?

Not seeing or hearing things, no… at least not like that.

The “targeting” part is harder to answer. I don’t want to sound dramatic, but there have been times where I felt pretty sure that people in the arts and finance circles here were paying attention to who I was meeting with—like client meetings—and then kind of sending little signals back through invitations or panel topics, or even who ended up sitting near me at events.

I can tell myself, “Okay, maybe that’s coincidence,” and I know that’s probably the reasonable answer… but I still can’t really let it go. So I don’t know if I’d say “completely certain” all the time, but it has felt very convincing at times. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Have you had experiences of hearing a voice speaking to you when no one was there?

No, I don’t think so. I haven’t had, like, a voice talking to me when no one’s there.

Sometimes I replay conversations in my head or worry about what people meant, but that’s not the same thing. So… no, I haven’t noticed anything like that.
Has there ever been a time when this belief felt completely fixed and certain to you for at least one full month?

Yeah… I think there was, though I feel a little uncomfortable saying it that strongly.

For at least a month, yes, it did feel pretty fixed to me that certain people in those arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati were tracking who I was meeting with—clients, especially—and sort of sending signals back through invitations, panel topics, or even who ended up near me at events.

I could tell myself, “Maybe it’s coincidence,” and I knew that’s what I probably should think… but honestly, during that time, I couldn’t really let it go. It felt very real to me. Is that what you mean by fixed and certain?
Since these changes first began, has there been a stretch of six months or more when you were having these kinds of symptoms or feeling noticeably unlike yourself?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, I wouldn’t want to make it sound like it’s been constant or that I’ve been completely not myself the whole time.

But these changes have been building since that arts nonprofit recognition, which was a little over two years ago now. So, yes, there’s definitely been more than six months where I’ve felt… different, or more caught up in these concerns than I used to be.

Does that answer what you’re asking?
Before these concerns about people tracking your client meetings began, had you long been seen by others as odd, eccentric, or unusually suspicious?

Um… I’m not sure I’d say that, no.

I mean, I’ve probably always been a little careful, maybe more private than some people, but I don’t think people would have described me as odd or eccentric. At least no one ever said that to me.

And “unusually suspicious” feels… stronger than I’d be comfortable agreeing with. Before all this, I think I came across pretty normal. Maybe a bit analytical, but not in a way that stood out. Does that make sense?

target_item.manifestation: I came in because for a while now I’ve been convinced that certain people in the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati are quietly tracking which clients I meet with and sending me little signals through invitations, panel topics, even who sits near me at events, and even when I tell myself it could just be coincidence, I can’t really let it go.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about psychotic experiences becoming more intense, especially feeling completely certain that people were targeting him, which directly relates to delusional beliefs.

patient.answer:
Not seeing or hearing things, no… at least not like that.

The “targeting” part is harder to answer. I don’t want to sound dramatic, but there have been times where I felt pretty sure that people in the arts and finance circles here were paying attention to who I was meeting with—like client meetings—and then kind of sending little signals back through invitations or panel topics, or even who ended up sitting near me at events.

I can tell myself, “Okay, maybe that’s coincidence,” and I know that’s probably the reasonable answer… but I still can’t really let it go. So I don’t know if I’d say “completely certain” all the time, but it has felt very convincing at times. Is that the kind of thing you mean?

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a clear period of persistent hallucinations or other first-rank psychotic symptoms, which would favor schizophrenia over schizotypal disorder and help distinguish from acute polymorphic psychosis.
doctor.question: Have you had experiences of hearing a voice speaking to you when no one was there?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about auditory hallucinations (hearing a voice when no one is there), which is not covered by the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
No, I don’t think so. I haven’t had, like, a voice talking to me when no one’s there.

Sometimes I replay conversations in my head or worry about what people meant, but that’s not the same thing. So… no, I haven’t noticed anything like that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has ever been a sustained period of clear psychotic symptoms lasting at least one month, which would help distinguish schizophrenia from schizotypal disorder and acute polymorphic psychotic disorder.
doctor.question: Has there ever been a time when this belief felt completely fixed and certain to you for at least one full month?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I came in because for a while now I’ve been convinced that certain people in the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati are quietly tracking which clients I meet with and sending me little signals through invitations, panel topics, even who sits near me at events, and even when I tell myself it could just be coincidence, I can’t really let it go.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the belief became fixed and certain for at least a month, which directly concerns delusions.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think there was, though I feel a little uncomfortable saying it that strongly.

For at least a month, yes, it did feel pretty fixed to me that certain people in those arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati were tracking who I was meeting with—clients, especially—and sort of sending signals back through invitations, panel topics, or even who ended up near me at events.

I could tell myself, “Maybe it’s coincidence,” and I knew that’s what I probably should think… but honestly, during that time, I couldn’t really let it go. It felt very real to me. Is that what you mean by fixed and certain?

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a continuous disturbance lasting at least 6 months, which would distinguish schizophrenia from schizophreniform disorder or acute transient psychotic disorder.
doctor.question: Since these changes first began, has there been a stretch of six months or more when you were having these kinds of symptoms or feeling noticeably unlike yourself?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: These changes have been building since that arts nonprofit recognition a little over two years ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether the overall changes/symptoms have persisted for six months or more since they first began, which directly matches the duration profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. I mean, I wouldn’t want to make it sound like it’s been constant or that I’ve been completely not myself the whole time.

But these changes have been building since that arts nonprofit recognition, which was a little over two years ago now. So, yes, there’s definitely been more than six months where I’ve felt… different, or more caught up in these concerns than I used to be.

Does that answer what you’re asking?

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has longstanding schizotypal personality features predating the recent psychotic belief, which would help distinguish schizotypal disorder from schizophrenia or acute psychotic disorder.
doctor.question: Before these concerns about people tracking your client meetings began, had you long been seen by others as odd, eccentric, or unusually suspicious?

target_item.reason: The question asks about whether others had long seen me as odd, eccentric, or unusually suspicious before the current tracking concerns began, which is not covered by the listed symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
Um… I’m not sure I’d say that, no.

I mean, I’ve probably always been a little careful, maybe more private than some people, but I don’t think people would have described me as odd or eccentric. At least no one ever said that to me.

And “unusually suspicious” feels… stronger than I’d be comfortable agreeing with. Before all this, I think I came across pretty normal. Maybe a bit analytical, but not in a way that stood out. Does that make sense?

inference.note: Longstanding negative symptoms/functional decline for >2 years plus at least 1 month of fixed persecutory delusion and overall disturbance >6 months support schizophrenia; premorbid odd/eccentric suspicious pattern was denied, arguing against F21; duration far exceeds acute/transient psychotic disorder, arguing against F23.3.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
opening_question.question: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a persecutory/referential delusional belief that arts and finance contacts are tracking client meetings and sending signals, with the belief fixed for at least one month and present most days for about two months. There is no evidence of hallucinations or formal thought disorder, but there are negative-symptom-like changes (reduced animation, social withdrawal, reduced speech, diminished interest) persisting over two years, and the patient confirms more than six months of feeling noticeably unlike himself. This pattern supports schizophrenia, paranoid type in ICD-10 (F20.0), over delusional disorder because of the longer prodromal/negative symptoms and broader functional/personality change. Schizotypal disorder was considered but is less likely because odd/eccentric or chronically suspicious premorbid traits were denied and the presentation includes a sustained fixed delusion.
